title: Acute Limb Ischemia: Medicare and Medicaid Reimbursement Gaps Threaten Sustainability of Care.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a vascular emergency associated with high morbidity and mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and substantial resource utilization. However, contemporary data evaluating the financial sustainability of ALI care across insurance types remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate hospitalization costs, reimbursement, profitability, and contribution margin (CM) for operative ALI care stratified by insurance status and revascularization strategy.

METHODS: A retrospective review of patients admitted with ALI at a quaternary medical center (2016-2024) was performed. Patients were identified using international classification of diseases-10 and currently procedural terminology codes. Exclusion criteria were outpatient encounters and nonoperative or nonprocedural management. Hospitalization cost was defined as the sum of variable and fixed costs. Profit was reimbursement minus cost. Analyses were stratified by insurance status and treatment modality. Continuous variables were compared using nonparametric tests, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05.

RESULTS: A total of 565 patients were included, of whom 60.2% were insured by Medicare, 24.2% by Medicaid, and 15.6% by commercial insurance. Median total hospitalization costs exceeded $50,000 per admission and did not differ by insurance status (Medicare $50,894 [interquartile range $33,496-$90,923], Medicaid $49,417 [$33,775-$83,379], commercial $56,603 [$35,823-$96,067]; P = 0.577) or by revascularization strategy (open versus endovascular; P > 0.05). Professional and technical cost components were similarly comparable across payer groups. Despite similar costs, reimbursement varied significantly by insurance status. Medicare and Medicaid admissions were associated with median hospital losses of -$12,673 [-$28,732 to -$1,425] and -$3,176 [-$10,035 to $3,859], respectively, while commercially insured admissions generated a median profit of $30,622 [$7,602-$50,208] (P < 0.001). These differences persisted across both open and endovascular subgroups.

CONCLUSION: Operative management of ALI is associated with substantial hospitalization costs that are consistent across revascularization strategies and payer types. While commercially insured admissions generated positive CMs, Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements were insufficient to offset costs. Given that most patients were insured through Medicare, the reimbursement disparities translated into an overall negative financial impact for ALI care. Without reimbursement reform or payment adjustment, the long-term financial sustainability of ALI care, and equitable patient access to timely revascularization, may be jeopardized.

However, contemporary data evaluating the financial sustainability of ALI care across insurance types remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate hospitalization costs, reimbursement, profitability, and contribution margin (CM) for operative ALI care stratified by insurance status and revascularization strategy.

title: A Vascular Surgery and Primary Care Partnership for Improving Resident Training in Peripheral Artery Disease Management.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early diagnosis, establishment of best medical management, and timely specialty referral for patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD) remain ongoing challenges. In this study, we sought to identify gaps in internal medicine (IM) and family medicine (FM) residents' self-rated competency of PAD management and investigated whether an educational session led by vascular surgeons could promote recognition and confidence in patient care.

METHODS: A single educational session, featuring a PowerPoint presentation, hands-on training (pulse and Doppler examination), and open discussion, was offered to IM and FM residents on two separate occasions. A presession survey assessed self-rated knowledge, practices, attitudes, and medical training regarding PAD, followed by a truncated postsession survey. The responses were grouped as high versus moderate/low. Descriptive statistics and the McNemar Exact test were used for paired sample comparison.

RESULTS: Thirty-one residents completed both surveys (65% IM, 35% FM, 58% male, and 77% first- or second-year trainees). Presession data revealed gaps in knowledge with few residents rating their understanding as "high". Postsession, there was a significant increase across all measured areas (P < 0.001). Notably, improvements were seen in the number of residents who felt highly confident in diagnosing PAD (from 16.1% to 90.3%), using a vascular Doppler (6.5% to 83.9%), ordering noninvasive testing (from 6.5% to 83.9%), performing a lower extremity pulse exam (from 12.9% to 87.1%), managing PAD for amputation prevention (from 12.9% to 71.0%), and referring to a vascular specialist (from 25.8% to 83.9%).

CONCLUSION: Resident knowledge and confidence improved significantly as a result of a singular educational session. This collaborative model between vascular surgery educators and primary care residency programs demonstrates an adaptable framework that successfully addresses a gap in PAD management training.

In this study, we sought to identify gaps in internal medicine (IM) and family medicine (FM) residents' self-rated competency of PAD management and investigated whether an educational session led by vascular surgeons could promote recognition and confidence in patient care. METHODS: A single educational session, featuring a PowerPoint presentation, hands-on training (pulse and Doppler examination), and open discussion, was offered to IM and FM residents on two separate occasions.

title: Calibrated Microspheres versus Liquid Embolic Agents for Chronic Subdural Hematoma: A Single-Center Clinicoradiologic Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAe) is an effective treatment for chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH), but the optimal embolic agent remains debated. Landmark randomized trials predominantly used liquid embolics, although calibrated microspheres remain widely used. We compared clinicoradiologic outcomes after MMAe with 75 μm Embozene microspheres versus liquid embolics (n-butyl cyanoacrylate or Onyx 18).

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed single-agent MMAe for cSDH at a tertiary center (January 2019-January 2025). The embolized MMA was the unit of analysis; agent choice was discretionary. The efficacy cohort required 2-8 week imaging (n = 66); the safety cohort included all single-agent procedures (n = 67; 35 particle, 32 liquid). Primary outcomes were embolization failure and unplanned surgical evacuation. Secondary outcomes included early SDH thickness, midline shift, and latest modified Rankin scale (mRS).

RESULTS: Fifty patients underwent 66 embolizations (16 bilateral): 34 particle and 32 liquid. Embolization failure occurred in 5/34 versus 4/32, and unplanned evacuation in 3/34 versus 1/32; events were few and the comparison underpowered. Female patients were more frequent in the particle group (47% vs. 19%, P = 0.020). Early SDH thickness was 8 (6) versus 6 (6) mm (P = 0.340). The safety cohort had one fatal posterior-circulation infarct after Embozene (1/35 vs. 0/32) and no other periprocedural complications.

CONCLUSIONS: Embolization failure was similar between 75 μm Embozene and liquid embolics, while unplanned evacuation was numerically higher with particles. Given infrequent events, limited sample size, and baseline imbalances, agent selection may be individualized by anatomy, visualization, and operator experience.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAe) is an effective treatment for chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH), but the optimal embolic agent remains debated. Landmark randomized trials predominantly used liquid embolics, although calibrated microspheres remain widely used. We compared clinicoradiologic outcomes after MMAe with 75 μm Embozene microspheres versus liquid embolics (n-butyl cyanoacrylate or Onyx 18).

title: Sepsis Prior to Total Knee Arthroplasty Is Associated With Elevated Rates of Myocardial Infarction and Deep Vein Thrombosis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients who have sepsis often experience persistent physiological instability, which may increase vulnerability to postoperative complications. However, the impact of preoperative sepsis on outcomes following elective total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains poorly defined. Thus, the purpose of this study was to investigate the association of preoperative sepsis with 90-day and two-year postoperative complications following TKA.

METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted utilizing an insurance database. Patients who had a preoperative diagnosis of sepsis within two years prior to TKA were matched at a 1:3 ratio to controls based on demographics and comorbidities. Patients who had sepsis were stratified according to the following timeline: sepsis three months prior to surgery, three to six months prior, six to 12 months prior, 12 to 18 months prior, and 18 to 24 months prior. Medical and surgical complications were assessed at 90 days and two years following surgery. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.

RESULTS: Patients who had sepsis within two years prior to surgery exhibited increased rates of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) (odds ratio (OR): 1.6), postoperative sepsis (OR: 2.7), acute kidney injury (OR: 1.4), urinary tract infection (OR: 1.8), blood transfusion (OR: 2.0), readmission (OR: 1.3), and wound dehiscence (OR: 1.4) within 90 days of surgery. At two years following surgery, sepsis was associated with elevated rates of revision surgery (OR: 1.3), PJI (OR: 1.6), osteomyelitis (OR: 1.9), and mortality (OR: 1.3). Sepsis within three months of operation was associated with elevated rates of myocardial infarction (OR: 2.1) and deep vein thrombosis (OR: 2.0). All findings were statistically significant at P < 0.05.

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative sepsis is associated with increased complications following TKA, including PJI and mortality. Sepsis within three months of surgery confers a particularly elevated risk of myocardial infarction and deep vein thrombosis following TKA.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Patients who have sepsis often experience persistent physiological instability, which may increase vulnerability to postoperative complications. However, the impact of preoperative sepsis on outcomes following elective total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains poorly defined. Thus, the purpose of this study was to investigate the association of preoperative sepsis with 90-day and two-year postoperative complications following TKA.

title: Early Outcomes of Thoracic Branch Endoprosthesis in Aortic Arch Pathologies: A Nordic Multicentre Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study evaluated the feasibility and early clinical outcomes of the Gore thoracic branch endoprosthesis (TBE) in the treatment of aortic arch pathologies.

METHODS: This multicentre retrospective study, conducted and reported in accordance with the STROBE statement, included consecutive patients undergoing thoracic endovascular aortic repair with TBE between February 2024 and July 2025. No restrictions were applied regarding the type or extent of aortic disease, use of staged procedures, or concomitant adjunctive endovascular interventions. Primary endpoints were technical success, thirty day death, and overall survival, while endoleak occurrence, primary target vessel patency, stroke, and spinal cord ischaemia (SCI) were secondary.

RESULTS: Sixty-four patients (median age 73 years [interquartile range {IQR} 59, 77]; 69% men) were included. Indications for treatment included degenerative aneurysm (n = 26; 41%), chronic dissection (n = 18; 28%), subacute dissection (n = 11; 17%), and acute dissection (n = 9; 14%). The left subclavian artery was the target vessel in 59 cases (92%), followed by the brachiocephalic trunk in three (5%) and the left common carotid artery in two (3%). Technical success was achieved in 95% of cases (n = 61), with failures attributed to two type Ia endoleaks and one type IIIa endoleak. The thirty day mortality rate was 3% (n = 2). Early unplanned re-interventions occurred in four patients (6%). No strokes or SCI were observed. Median follow up was 6 months (IQR 2, 10). There were no late deaths, and primary patency of all branches was 100%. One late unplanned re-intervention, unrelated to the TBE device, was required. During follow up, 12 patients (19%) had endoleaks, including type II (n = 4), type Ia (n = 4), type Ib (n = 2), type III (n = 1), and type V (n = 1). Estimated freedom from type Ia endoleak at 12 months was 93 ± 3%, while estimated overall survival at 12 months was 97 ± 2%.

CONCLUSION: TBE demonstrated high technical success and acceptable early outcomes across a range of aortic arch pathologies. However, the relatively high rate of endoleaks and need for early re-interventions highlight the importance of careful patient selection and close continuous post-operative surveillance.

METHODS: This multicentre retrospective study, conducted and reported in accordance with the STROBE statement, included consecutive patients undergoing thoracic endovascular aortic repair with TBE between February 2024 and July 2025. No restrictions were applied regarding the type or extent of aortic disease, use of staged procedures, or concomitant adjunctive endovascular interventions.

title: Multidisciplinary Collaboration in the Performance of Aortic Surgery: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
abstract: Intraoperative management of a patient undergoing cardiac surgery requires continuous and independent interventions by multiple healthcare professionals, including surgeons, anesthesiologists, and perfusionists, among others. Although each clinician performs tasks based on their training and accepted techniques, guidelines, and protocols, an action by one member of the team can have immediate consequences for other team members. Aortic surgery adds a level of complexity, with the need for interventions such as single-lung ventilation, systemic cooling (and subsequent rewarming), and myocardial, cerebral, and visceral protection. Much has been made of the utility of the multidisciplinary team. This scientific statement is intended to approach the patient undergoing aortic surgery from 3 different viewpoints: that of the surgeon, the anesthesiologist, and the perfusionist. This scientific statement is not intended to provide an exhaustive summary of approaches to aortic surgery but rather to illustrate the specific concerns that each member of the team may have.

title: Emergency Endovascular Repair of a Large Ruptured Isolated Internal Iliac Artery Aneurysm in a 98-Year-Old Patient: A Case Report.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Isolated internal iliac artery aneurysm (IIAA) is rare and carries a high mortality when ruptured. Management is particularly challenging in very elderly, anticoagulated patients in whom open repair may carry substantial perioperative risk. Herein, we report a case that illustrates device selection when a marked common iliac-external iliac size discrepancy precludes bridging with the available iliac limbs. Case Presentation: A 98-year-old man receiving apixaban presented with lower abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea. Computed tomography demonstrated a ruptured right IIAA measuring 79 × 72 mm in the axial plane, with retroperitoneal hematoma. A marked size discrepancy between the common iliac artery (20 mm) and external iliac artery (approximately 10 mm), together with vessel tortuosity, made common iliac-external iliac bridging with an iliac limb unsuitable with the devices available. Emergency endovascular aneurysm repair with a full aortic bifurcated endograft was combined with coil embolization of the inferior gluteal artery and gelatin sponge embolization of the sac. The contralateral internal iliac artery, which harbored a 31 mm aneurysm, was preserved. A suspected type IV endoleak had resolved on CT at day 4, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 8 without complications. At 6-month follow-up, the aneurysm sac had decreased from 79 × 72 mm to 72 × 62 mm in the axial plane with no evidence of endoleak, and he remained ambulatory without pelvic ischemic symptoms. Conclusions: A full aortic bifurcated endograft combined with coil and sac embolization may be a feasible bail-out option when a marked common iliac-external iliac size discrepancy precludes bridging with the available iliac limbs, even in a nonagenarian receiving apixaban.
englishSummary: Background/Objectives: Isolated internal iliac artery aneurysm (IIAA) is rare and carries a high mortality when ruptured. Management is particularly challenging in very elderly, anticoagulated patients in whom open repair may carry substantial perioperative risk. Herein, we report a case that illustrates device selection when a marked common iliac-external iliac size discrepancy precludes bridging with the available iliac limbs.

title: Patient Selection and Evidence for Intervention in Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract: Intervention for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) should address a clinical problem that anticoagulation alone may not resolve. This narrative review separates whether to intervene, which procedure to choose, and how to maintain benefit. The review covers publications through 10 September 2026, with a later STORM-PE follow-up report identified separately. Anticoagulation remains foundational. In acute iliofemoral DVT, selected patients may gain earlier symptom relief or less severe post-thrombotic disease, but trials do not support routine thrombus removal. In established post-thrombotic obstruction, C-TRACT showed better six-month clinical severity and quality of life with stenting and enhanced antithrombotic treatment, alongside more bleeding. In selected stable PE, HI-PEITHO reduced a seven-day clinical composite from 10.3% to 4.0%, mainly through fewer episodes of decompensation; a survival benefit remains unproven. Procedure comparisons and imaging trials answer narrower questions than benefit over medical care. Limb-threatening DVT and unstable PE require urgent rescue assessment. A five-scenario table and clinical examples connect this evidence to symptoms, anatomy, recovery goals, bleeding risk, and the feasibility of continuing treatment and follow-up.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Cannulation of Arteriovenous Fistulas in Hemodialysis Units: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Arteriovenous fistulas are the preferred vascular access for hemodialysis, but difficult or unsuccessful cannulation may cause pain, complications, and access dysfunction. This review evaluated whether ultrasound-guided cannulation improves outcomes compared with standard cannulation. Methods: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for randomized controlled trials comparing ultrasound-guided and standard arteriovenous fistula cannulation in hemodialysis patients. Findings were synthesized narratively. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Results: Of 1210 records identified, five randomized trials involving 142 patients were included. Some trials reported improved cannulation success or lower pain with ultrasound guidance, but findings varied across populations and outcome measures. Three of four trials reporting procedure time found longer durations with ultrasound guidance. A consistent reduction in complications or improvement in patient satisfaction was not established. Staff findings mainly concerned confidence and acceptability. The certainty of evidence was low. Conclusions: The effects of ultrasound-guided AVF cannulation on pain varied across trials. These uncertain findings should be interpreted alongside the longer procedure times reported in several trials. Larger randomized trials with clearly defined outcomes and analyses accounting for repeated observations are needed before recommending routine use.

title: Preprocedural Serum Albumin and Early Contrast-Associated Acute Kidney Injury After Elective Carotid Artery Stenting: Incremental Prognostic Information Beyond the PCI-Derived Mehran Score.
abstract: Background/Objectives: We assessed whether preprocedural serum albumin adds prognostic information to the PCI-derived Mehran score for early contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) after elective carotid artery stenting (CAS). Methods: This single-centre retrospective cohort included 121 consecutive elective patients (January 2020-April 2026). The primary model combined the reconstructed Mehran score with albumin < 3.5 g/dL, a conventional threshold fixed in advance. Because the score uses actual contrast volume, the combined model applies only after CAS. The outcome used KDIGO serum creatinine thresholds (≥0.3 mg/dL or ≥1.5 times baseline) from routine second-day testing. Internal validation used 1000 bootstrap resamples. Results: Early CA-AKI occurred in 32 patients (26.4%). Adjusted odds ratios were 1.35 per Mehran point (95% CI 1.13-1.60) and 11.68 for albumin < 3.5 g/dL (95% CI 4.14-32.97). AUC increased from 0.768 to 0.865 (95% CI 0.794-0.937; likelihood ratio χ2 = 24.58, p < 0.001). Corrected AUC, calibration slope, and Brier score were 0.860, 0.96, and 0.132. In exploratory decision curves (20% threshold), corrected net benefit was 0.168 for the combined model and 0.133 for Mehran alone. Conclusions: Low preprocedural albumin added prognostic information to the PCI-derived score and may help select patients for closer renal surveillance after CAS. External validation and prospective impact studies are needed before clinical use.

The primary model combined the reconstructed Mehran score with albumin < 3.5 g/dL, a conventional threshold fixed in advance.

title: Role of direct intraoperative ultrasound-guided renal resistive index and its association with postoperative acute kidney injury in patients undergoing abdominal vascular surgeries: A prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a major complication following abdominal vascular surgery, and current diagnostic markers often detect injury only after significant renal damage has occurred. Doppler-derived renal resistive index (RRI) is a promising real-time marker of renal perfusion. This study evaluated direct intraoperative ultrasound (DIOUS)-guided RRI measurement for assessing postoperative AKI in open abdominal vascular surgery.

METHODS: In this prospective study, 40 adults undergoing open abdominal vascular procedures were enroled. RRI was measured at four timepoints: preoperatively; intraoperatively, 30 minutes after aortic declamping, using DIOUS; and postoperatively at 12 and 24 hours using transabdominal Doppler ultrasonography. AKI was defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes creatinine-based criteria.

RESULTS: Postoperative AKI developed in 50% of patients. Mean DIOUS-guided RRI measured 30 minutes after declamping was higher in patients who developed AKI than in those who did not (0.74 ± 0.05 vs. 0.69 ± 0.04; P = 0.003). Receiver operating characteristic analysis identified an exploratory, internally derived intraoperative RRI cut-off of 0.71, predicting postoperative AKI with 80% sensitivity and 70% specificity [area under curve 0.783; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.639-0.927]. The odds of developing AKI increased by 33% for every 0.01-unit increase in intraoperative RRI (odds ratio 1.33; 95% CI 1.03-1.71; P = 0.026).

CONCLUSION: DIOUS-guided RRI measurement is a feasible method for real-time assessment of renal haemodynamics during open abdominal vascular surgery. The association between intraoperative RRI and postoperative AKI suggests this technique may complement perioperative renal risk assessment and support early kidney-protective interventions, pending validation in larger studies.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a major complication following abdominal vascular surgery, and current diagnostic markers often detect injury only after significant renal damage has occurred. Doppler-derived renal resistive index (RRI) is a promising real-time marker of renal perfusion. This study evaluated direct intraoperative ultrasound (DIOUS)-guided RRI measurement for assessing postoperative AKI in open abdominal vascular surgery.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of magnetic resonance calcification imaging for lower-extremity peripheral artery disease.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent advances in magnetic resonance imaging-based bone imaging techniques may help visualize vascular calcification, and their combination with noncontrast magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) can facilitate a comprehensive, noninvasive assessment of lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) without contrast media or ionizing radiation.

METHODS: Forty-three patients with lower-extremity PAD who underwent magnetic resonance calcification imaging (MRCI) and noncontrast MRA before endovascular intervention between November 2022 and June 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. The aortoiliac and femoropopliteal arteries were divided into 10 segments on MRCI and assessed for calcification using computed tomography images as reference standards. Calcification in each segment was graded using the Peripheral Arterial Calcium Scoring System. Calcification characteristics and lumen diameters on MRCI were compared with those obtained using intravascular ultrasound (IVUS).

RESULTS: Renal insufficiency was observed in 30 of 43 patients (69.8%); 24 (55.8%) had claudication, and 16 (37.2%) had chronic limb-threatening ischemia. Weighted Cohen κ coefficients demonstrated substantial to almost perfect agreement between MRCI and computed tomography in the assessment of vascular calcification (reader 1: κ = .89; reader 2: κ = .80). In 13 patients with 24 femoropopliteal lesions (≥50% stenosis) evaluated by IVUS, MRCI demonstrated close agreement with IVUS for both calcification angles (mean difference, 1.3°; 95% limits of agreement, -19.1° to 21.8°) and lumen diameter (short axis, -0.05 mm; 95% limits of agreement, -0.46 to 0.36 mm; long axis, -0.06 mm; 95% limits of agreement, -0.67 to 0.55 mm).

CONCLUSIONS: MRCI provides quantitative, noninvasive depiction of vascular calcification, and, when combined with noncontrast MRA, may provide complementary information for the imaging assessment of lower-extremity PAD without contrast media or ionizing radiation. Future larger prospective multicenter studies are needed to confirm these findings and to further define the clinical role of this imaging approach.

METHODS: Forty-three patients with lower-extremity PAD who underwent magnetic resonance calcification imaging (MRCI) and noncontrast MRA before endovascular intervention between November 2022 and June 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. The aortoiliac and femoropopliteal arteries were divided into 10 segments on MRCI and assessed for calcification using computed tomography images as reference standards.

title: Risk factors and clinical outcomes of reocclusion after endovascular treatment for acute ischemic stroke: an updated systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly defined.

METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE. Post hoc sensitivity analyses included only same-site reocclusion definitions.

RESULTS: Ten studies (3,381 patients) were included; 244 (7.2%) reoccluded. Reocclusion was associated with lower 90-day functional independence (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.17-0.38) and higher mortality (OR 1.86, 1.29-2.68), both moderate certainty. Reocclusion was more frequent with large-artery atherosclerosis (OR 2.24, 1.41-3.55; same-site 3.04, 1.73-5.33) and less frequent with cardioembolism (OR 0.40, 0.28-0.57) and atrial fibrillation (OR 0.39, 0.26-0.59), mutually confounded associations reflecting one embolic-versus-atherothrombotic axis. Prestroke antiplatelet therapy (OR 0.43, 0.28-0.67) lost significance under the same-site definition (0.60, 0.31-1.16). Exploratory data (two cohorts) linked eTICI 2c-3 reperfusion with less reocclusion (OR 0.44, 0.28-0.69). No study reported when etiology was adjudicated; the atherosclerosis association may be partly outcome-induced.

CONCLUSIONS: Early reocclusion is uncommon but carries a substantial prognostic penalty. Its determinants appear to lie in the vascular substrate rather than thrombectomy technique; prospective studies with uniform same-site definitions and systematic follow-up imaging are needed.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly defined. METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE.

title: Deep Learning-Based 3D CT Body Composition Is Associated With Mortality in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recent advances in artificial intelligence enable fully automated 3-dimensional computed tomography (CT)-based body composition quantification. We investigated whether automated CT-derived thoraco-abdominopelvic body composition measures are associated with mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, consecutive patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement with preprocedural CT imaging were included between 2014 and 2023. A deep learning-based pipeline performed automated 3-dimensional segmentation of thoraco-abdominopelvic noncontrast CT scans to quantify volumes (L/m2) and attenuations (Hounsfield units) of subcutaneous adipose tissue, visceral adipose tissue, muscular adipose tissue, and lean skeletal muscle, indexed to body surface area. Associations with mortality were evaluated using Cox models and Harrell C statistics, adjusting for demographics (age, sex, body mass index) and cardiometabolic risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, chronic renal failure).

RESULTS: Among 915 patients (median age, 84 years [interquartile range, 77-90]; 58% men), 160 (17.5%) died over a median follow-up of 22 months (interquartile range, 14-36). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated that lower subcutaneous adipose tissue volume and higher adipose tissue attenuation were associated with increased mortality, whereas higher skeletal muscle volume and attenuation were associated with improved survival. Addition of body composition measures provided incremental discriminatory value beyond demographics and cardiometabolic risk factors (Harrell C, 0.66 versus 0.71; P<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Automated 3-dimensional CT-derived body composition measures provide independent prognostic information and improve risk stratification for mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. Low subcutaneous adipose tissue volume and higher adipose tissue attenuation identify patients at increased risk, whereas higher skeletal muscle volume and attenuation are associated with lower mortality.

We investigated whether automated CT-derived thoraco-abdominopelvic body composition measures are associated with mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, consecutive patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement with preprocedural CT imaging were included between 2014 and 2023.

title: Anti-Ro-Positive Lupus-Like Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome After BNT162b2 COVID-19 Vaccination: A Case Report.
abstract: Rare immune-mediated syndromes following COVID-19 vaccination have been described across a heterogeneous clinical spectrum. Anti-Ro/SSA-positive multisystem presentations with features of undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) or subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) remain under-reported. A 66-year-old Caucasian man with no prior autoimmune history developed a progressive multisystem inflammatory illness approximately 14 days after receiving his second dose of the BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) COVID-19 vaccine. Clinical features included an erythematous malar and dorsal rash, pharyngitis, geographic tongue, constitutional upset with profound fatigue, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of 12 kg. Investigations revealed normocytic anaemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and bilateral pleural effusions. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) demonstrated metabolically active mediastinal, supraclavicular, and pelvic lymphadenopathy with increased bone marrow and splenic uptake. Autoimmune serology showed a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test and strongly positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, with negative anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies, normal complement levels, and negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). Extensive investigation excluded malignancy, infection, sarcoidosis, and classical systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). A lower limb deep vein thrombosis developed during hospitalisation. Systemic corticosteroids produced clear and sustained clinical and radiological improvement. The serological and clinical phenotype (anti-Ro-positive, anti-dsDNA-negative, complement-normal, without nephritis) is most consistent with UCTD or SCLE with systemic involvement rather than classical SLE. This case contributes to the emerging literature on post-vaccination autoimmunity, emphasises the importance of precise serological phenotyping, and highlights the need for structured long-term follow-up to determine whether such presentations represent transient immune dysregulation or the onset of persistent connective tissue disease.

Anti-Ro/SSA-positive multisystem presentations with features of undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) or subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) remain under-reported. A 66-year-old Caucasian man with no prior autoimmune history developed a progressive multisystem inflammatory illness approximately 14 days after receiving his second dose of the BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) COVID-19 vaccine.

title: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Disease-Specific Quality of Life After Surgical and Conservative Treatments for Lower Limb Varicose Veins: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Lower limb varicose veins are a common manifestation of chronic venous disease and can adversely affect physical functioning, symptom burden, and disease-specific quality of life (QoL). Although high ligation and stripping have traditionally been considered standard surgical approaches, conservative and minimally invasive options, such as compression therapy, sclerotherapy, and endovenous thermal or non-thermal techniques, have increasingly gained prominence. However, comparative evidence regarding patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) remains heterogeneous and dispersed across randomized trials. This systematic review aimed to evaluate randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2016 and 2026 that compared surgical with conservative or minimally invasive interventions for lower limb varicose veins, with particular emphasis on patient-reported and disease-specific QoL outcomes. The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. PubMed/Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), Scopus, Web of Science, Excerpta Medica database (Embase), the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar were searched for eligible RCTs published from January 2016 to July 2026. Studies evaluating surgical versus conservative or minimally invasive management and reporting PROMs or disease-specific QoL outcomes were included. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively in accordance with Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidance. Fourteen RCTs met the eligibility criteria. Interventions included open surgery, endovenous laser ablation (EVLA), radiofrequency ablation (RFA), mechanochemical ablation (MOCA), cyanoacrylate adhesive closure, ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (UGFS), and compression therapy. Improvements in disease-specific QoL and PROMs were reported from baseline in most treatment groups. However, these within-group improvements did not necessarily indicate superiority over alternative treatments. Between-group differences in QoL outcomes were generally small and inconsistent, although some trials reported differences in procedural pain, anatomical outcomes, or the need for re-intervention. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. Surgical, conservative, and minimally invasive approaches were associated with meaningful improvements in patient-reported and disease-specific QoL, with no consistent evidence demonstrating clear superiority of one modality. Treatment decisions should therefore incorporate anatomical suitability, patient preference, procedural morbidity, potential need for re-intervention, and healthcare resource considerations alongside QoL outcomes.
englishSummary: Lower limb varicose veins are a common manifestation of chronic venous disease and can adversely affect physical functioning, symptom burden, and disease-specific quality of life (QoL). Although high ligation and stripping have traditionally been considered standard surgical approaches, conservative and minimally invasive options, such as compression therapy, sclerotherapy, and endovenous thermal or non-thermal techniques, have increasingly gained prominence. However, comparative evidence regarding patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) remains heterogeneous and dispersed across randomized trials.

title: Primary Aortoduodenal Fistula: A Case Report and Recent Literature Review (2021-2025).
abstract: Primary aortoduodenal fistula (PADF) is a rare but life-threatening cause of gastrointestinal bleeding, most commonly resulting from an abdominal aortic aneurysm eroding into the duodenum. Diagnosis is particularly challenging because of its nonspecific clinical presentation and the limited sensitivity and technical challenges of endoscopy. We present the case of an 89-year-old man with significant cardiovascular comorbidities, who developed acute abdominal pain and transient malaise, followed by massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding leading to hemorrhagic shock. Initial management included aggressive resuscitation with crystalloids, vasopressors, and initiation of a massive hemorrhage protocol. Due to severe hemodynamic instability, we could not perform a computed tomography angiography (CTA), and the patient underwent emergent laparotomy. Intraoperative upper endoscopy via surgical gastrostomy revealed a fistula between the infrarenal aorta and the fourth portion of the duodenum. Surgical intervention included end-to-end aorto-aortic bypass with a prosthetic graft, and primary duodenal repair with omental interposition. The postoperative course was complicated by ischemic colitis, respiratory failure, and progressive multi-organ failure. Despite maximal supportive measures, the patient's condition deteriorated, and care was ultimately transitioned to comfort-focused management. In our review, one key finding is the increasing trend toward endovascular and hybrid approaches for managing PADF. These strategies may facilitate more rapid hemodynamic stabilization in critically ill patients. More recently, exclusively endovascular or endoscopic procedures have been reported as potential destination therapies in carefully selected cases, particularly when conventional open repair is not feasible. PADF remains a surgical emergency with a high risk of mortality. This case highlights the importance of early recognition, aggressive resuscitation, and prompt surgical intervention. Multidisciplinary collaboration and individualized decision-making, including consideration of hybrid endovascular and open techniques, are essential to optimize outcomes in this rare but catastrophic condition.

title: Aspirin-Based Thromboprophylaxis Versus Anticoagulant Regimens After Total Hip or Knee Arthroplasty: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Aspirin is widely used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis after total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA); however, uncertainty remains regarding its efficacy and safety compared with anticoagulant regimens. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated aspirin-based thromboprophylaxis versus anticoagulant regimens following THA or TKA. Materials and Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched through July 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing aspirin-based prophylaxis with anticoagulant regimens. The primary outcomes were any deep vein thrombosis (DVT), symptomatic DVT, and symptomatic venous thromboembolism (VTE). Secondary outcomes included pulmonary embolism (PE), proximal and distal DVT, bleeding outcomes, wound complications, blood transfusion, and mortality. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Additional risk-difference sensitivity analyses incorporated CRISTAL's published cluster-adjusted estimates. Results: Sixteen trials involving 21,265 participants were included. Aspirin was associated with higher risks of symptomatic DVT (RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.35-2.38), symptomatic VTE (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.33-2.18), PE (RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.33-2.68), and distal DVT (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.06-2.06). Aspirin was associated with lower risks of minor bleeding (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31-0.71) and ecchymosis or bruising (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.93). No statistically significant differences were detected for the other assessed outcomes. Additional analyses incorporating CRISTAL's cluster-adjusted risk differences did not identify statistically significant differences for the three primary outcomes or PE. Conclusions: The main pooled analyses associated aspirin-based thromboprophylaxis with higher risks of symptomatic thromboembolic events. However, the symptomatic DVT and symptomatic VTE associations were no longer statistically significant after exclusion of CRISTAL or restriction to trials at low risk of bias. The low-risk analysis identified a significantly higher risk of any DVT with aspirin. Aspirin reduced minor bleeding and bruising without a statistically significant reduction in major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding. These findings require cautious interpretation given dependence on CRISTAL, sensitivity to trial inclusion and analytical approach, and differences in prophylactic strategies and outcome definitions.

title: Early and follow-up results of reinterventions for type 2 endoleak following endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm in the multicenter Reinterventions for Type 2 Endoleak study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Type II endoleak (T2EL) is frequent after endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair and may require reintervention in selected patients. However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains uncertain. This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the perioperative and long-term outcomes of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open surgical, in a large patient cohort from 20 high-volume academic centers.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis of consecutive patients undergoing first reintervention for T2ELs was conducted across 20 centers over a 10-year period. Patients requiring concomitant treatment for other endoleak types were excluded. A total of 403 patients were included. Primary outcomes included technical success, 30-day AAA-related mortality and reintervention-free survival during follow-up. Secondary outcomes were perioperative complications, early reintervention, overall survival, freedom from aneurysm-related death and rupture, freedom from recurrent endoleaks, freedom from open conversion or semiconversion in patients previously treated endovascularly and sac behavior during follow-up. Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression analyses were performed to analyze follow-up results.

RESULTS: Patients were predominantly male (90%) with a mean age of 77 years. Reintervention was indicated for sac enlargement in 94.5% of cases; 4% presented with rupture. Median time from endovascular AAA repair to reintervention was 4.3 years. Lumbar arteries (55%) and the inferior mesenteric artery (35%) were the main sources. Endovascular treatment was performed in 86% and open conversion/semiconversion in 14%. Technical success was 96%, with 1% mortality and 4% major complications. Overall survival was 80.5% and rupture-free survival 79.2% at 5 years. Recurrent T2EL occurred in 64.2%, and reintervention-free survival was 48.3%. Endovascular group showed significantly lower freedom from reintervention rates when compared to open conversion/semiconversion group [42.4% vs 86.8%; standard error, 0.04 vs standard error, 0.05; P < .001; log-rank, 15.9]. Conversion/semiconversion after endovascular treatment occurred in 14%. No differences were recorded comparing different fabric materials of the endograft in terms of freedom for reintervention and freedom from open surgery. A sac diameter ≥7 cm at the time of reintervention predicted further reinterventions, whereas primary open treatment improved durability.

CONCLUSIONS: Reinterventions for T2ELs are safe, with satisfactory immediate technical success and low perioperative mortality. During follow-up, risks of rupture and AAA-related death remain low. However, the endoleak recurrence rate exceeds 60% at 5 years, necessitating reintervention in over 40% of patients. Early intervention for patients with a sac diameter approaching 7 cm can be suggested, whereas a primary open approach may be considered in low-risk patients.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Type II endoleak (T2EL) is frequent after endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair and may require reintervention in selected patients. However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains uncertain. This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the perioperative and long-term outcomes of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open surgical, in a large patient cohort from 20 high-volume academic centers.

title: Cerebral blood flow-oxygen metabolism uncoupling at 24 hours after stroke thrombectomy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Following successful endovascular therapy (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke, tissue with abnormal perfusion may have impaired oxygen extraction and metabolism. MRI model-based oxygen extraction fraction (OEFmax) and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) were characterized in hypoperfusion and hyperemia regions 24 h post-EVT.

METHODS: Eighty-four patients were included with anterior circulation vessel occlusion, successful recanalization, and an MRI at 24 h post-EVT. Time-to-maximum (Tmax) and cerebral blood flow (CBF) were evaluated for hypoperfusion and hyperemia. CBF, OEFmax, and CMRO2 were quantified using (i) segmentation-based and (ii) single slice region of interest (ROI) analyses. Normalized CBF, OEFmax, and CMRO2 were calculated by dividing the segmentation or ROI value by the contralateral value.

RESULTS: Sixty-seven (80%) patients had abnormal perfusion; hypoperfusion in 22 (26%), hyperemia in 36 (43%), and both in 9 (11%). Compared to control, hypoperfused regions demonstrated a 62% CBF decrease, 52% CMRO2 decrease, and 68% OEFmax increase (p < 0.01). Hyperemic regions demonstrated a 58% CBF increase, 26% CMRO2 increase, and 25% OEFmax decrease (p < 0.01). Hyperemia had no significant correlation between normalized CBF and CMRO2 (p = 0.14).

CONCLUSION: Hyperemia regions demonstrated cerebral blood flow-oxygen metabolism uncoupling, suggesting the underlying mechanism as loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation rather than hypermetabolic demand.

MRI model-based oxygen extraction fraction (OEFmax) and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) were characterized in hypoperfusion and hyperemia regions 24 h post-EVT. METHODS: Eighty-four patients were included with anterior circulation vessel occlusion, successful recanalization, and an MRI at 24 h post-EVT.

title: Study protocol of a prospective, non-interventional cohort study evaluating the benefits of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma receiving first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (NISTIPS TRITICC-4, IKF092).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, with most patients diagnosed at an advanced stage. Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab is a current standard first-line therapy; however, outcomes are strongly influenced by underlying cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH). Complications such as ascites and variceal bleeding may limit treatment continuation, particularly as bevacizumab increases bleeding risk. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) reduces portal pressure and may improve outcomes, but its role in patients receiving immunoncology-based systemic therapy remains unclear.

METHODS: NISTIPS TRITICC-4 is a prospective, multicentre, non-interventional cohort study conducted at up to 25 centers in Germany. A total of 350 adult patients with cirrhosis and unresectable or metastatic HCC receiving first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab will be enrolled. Patients are allocated to two cohorts: TIPS in situ plus atezolizumab and bevacizumab or atezolizumab plus bevacizumab alone, according to routine clinical practice.The primary endpoint is time to deterioration of liver function (TTDL), defined as persistent worsening of liver parameters for >4 weeks. Secondary endpoints include overall survival, time on treatment, overall response rate, time to new extrahepatic lesions or death, and safety with focus on bleeding and TIPS-related complications.Time-to-event endpoints will be analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox models. Propensity score matching will be applied to adjust for confounding. Analyses are exploratory.

DISCUSSION: This study will provide real-world evidence on the impact of TIPS in HCC patients receiving atezolizumab plus bevacizumab and may support more individualized management strategies in this high-risk population.

title: Heterogeneity in Time-Outcome Associations After Endovascular Thrombectomy: A Binational Registry Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although "time is brain" remains a core principle in acute stroke care, the association between treatment timing and functional outcomes after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) varies across patients. Some individuals treated in extended time windows still achieve favorable outcomes, a phenomenon termed the "late window paradox." Differences in stroke pathophysiology across etiologies may contribute to heterogeneity in the time-outcome relationship after EVT. We investigated factors associated with heterogeneity in time-dependent EVT responsiveness, with particular attention to stroke etiology.

METHODS: We analyzed data from two multicenter registries in Korea (CRCS-K) and Taiwan (TREAT-AIS) from January 2019 to April 2023. Patients with anterior circulation acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism (CE) or large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) were included. Multivariable regression and interaction analyzes were performed to evaluate the association between onset-to-puncture (OTP) time and 90-day functional outcomes and to identify effect modifiers.

RESULTS: Among 4,719 patients (mean age 72.0 years; 42.9% women; median NIHSS 15), longer OTP time was associated with lower odds of 90-day functional independence (adjusted OR per hour, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.96-0.98; p = 0.001). The impact of OTP time varied by stroke characteristics. CE etiology, MCA occlusion, higher NIHSS, and male sex were associated with greater time sensitivity. In CE strokes, each hour of delay reduced the odds of functional independence by 4% (aOR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.94-0.97; p < 0.001), whereas no significant association was observed in LAA strokes (P_interaction=0.028).

CONCLUSION: The association between EVT timing and functional outcome varies according to stroke etiology and clinical characteristics, highlighting heterogeneity in time-outcome relationships among EVT-treated patients and providing observational insight into outcome variability in extended treatment windows.

title: Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt as a Cause of Recurrent Encephalopathy in a Non-cirrhotic Patient: Successful Combined Transhepatic and Transjugular Embolization.
abstract: Intrahepatic portosystemic shunts (IPSS) are rare vascular anomalies that can cause recurrent encephalopathy in non-cirrhotic patients. We present a case of a female with recurrent episodes of delirium, in whom initial laboratory tests showed hyperammonemia with preserved hepatic function. Cross-sectional imaging revealed a left-sided IPSS connecting distal branches of the left portal vein to the left hepatic vein. Given her persistent neurocognitive symptoms despite optimal medical therapy, endovascular closure was performed using a dual-access strategy: transhepatic coil embolization of the portal afferent branches, followed by transjugular deployment of an Amplatzer plug in the venous outflow. After the procedure, the patient experienced full resolution of symptoms, with no recurrent neurological episodes during follow-up. This case highlights the importance of considering IPSS as a reversible cause of unexplained encephalopathy and supports the efficacy of combined-access embolization.

title: Caprini Score-Guided Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Spine Instrumentation Surgery: A Comparative Analysis of Mechanical vs. Pharmacomechanical Strategies Across Etiological Subgroups.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), encompassing deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is a major source of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing spine surgery. Although various risk factors for developing VTE have been identified, pharmacological prophylaxis is used selectively in spine surgery due to the risk of epidural hematoma. We report our institutional experience with VTE prophylaxis following spine instrumentation surgery across all surgical etiologies.

METHODS: A single-center retrospective cohort study of patients ≥18 years of age who underwent spine instrumentation surgery for degenerative, traumatic, or oncologic pathologies, and patients of all ages who underwent surgery for spinal deformity over a three-year period was performed. Caprini VTE risk score was used for individual risk stratification.

RESULTS: A total of 265 patients were included: degenerative (n=174, 65.7%), trauma (n=45, 17.0%), deformity (n=33, 12.5%), and tumor (n=13, 4.9%). The overall mean age was 46.1±17.5 years, and there were 133 male patients (50.2%). Significant differences existed across groups in age (Kruskal-Wallis H=97.4, p<0.001), index procedure characteristics, and VTE risk profiles. Mechanical prophylaxis alone was employed in 212 patients (80.0%), while 53 patients (20.0%) received combined pharmacomechanical prophylaxis. No patient (0%) in the mechanical-only group developed a perioperative VTE event or postoperative hematoma. One patient (1.9%) in the combined pharmacomechanical group developed a postoperative PE, arising in the context of a preoperative proximal DVT. Firth's penalized logistic regression identified polytrauma (OR 29.0, 95% CI 3.3-3835.0; p=0.001), Caprini score ≥7 (OR 8.8, 95% CI 3.8-20.9; p<0.001), and prior VTE history (OR 61.8, 95% CI 5.7-8406.4; p<0.001) as independent predictors of combined prophylaxis receipt.

CONCLUSION: Mechanical prophylaxis, implemented as part of a structured protocol that included sequential pneumatic compression devices and standardized postoperative care, was associated with low VTE risk following spine instrumentation surgery. Individualized risk stratification using validated tools such as the Caprini score, combined with selective pharmacomechanical prophylaxis in high-risk patients, may optimize outcomes in this population. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to validate these findings.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), encompassing deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is a major source of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing spine surgery. Although various risk factors for developing VTE have been identified, pharmacological prophylaxis is used selectively in spine surgery due to the risk of epidural hematoma. We report our institutional experience with VTE prophylaxis following spine instrumentation surgery across all surgical etiologies.

title: Postpartum "Hypercoagulable Storm" With Extensive Iliocaval Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism in a Patient With Heterozygous Factor V Leiden.
abstract: A 26-year-old woman presented to the emergency department four weeks after a lower segment cesarean section with a four-day history of progressive dyspnea, bilateral lower limb swelling, and leg pain. At presentation to the emergency department, she was tachycardic (150 beats/min), hypotensive (88/60 mmHg), and tachypneic (38/min), with an oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. Venous Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral deep vein thrombosis (DVT) involving the iliac veins, right external iliac vein, infrarenal inferior vena cava (IVC), and right popliteal vein, with left popliteal involvement. Computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute pulmonary embolism (PE) involving the right pulmonary artery and multiple segmental branches, with right lower lobe pulmonary infarction. Thrombophilia evaluation identified heterozygous Factor V Leiden, with negative antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant and normal protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels. The initial presentation raised concern for high-risk acute pulmonary embolism physiology, with hypotension (88/60 mmHg), marked tachycardia, and respiratory compromise requiring high-flow oxygen. Category D1+R was considered provisionally; however, definitive classification was limited by the absence of documented hypotension duration and fluid responsiveness, lactate, echocardiographic right ventricular assessment, and computed tomography (CT) right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio. A Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) was activated, and intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH) was initiated. A retrievable suprarenal IVC filter was placed, followed by mechanical thrombectomy extending from the right popliteal vein to the IVC. At three months, the patient remained ambulatory without exertional dyspnea, and bilateral lower limb swelling had completely resolved. Repeat venous Doppler demonstrated recanalization of the previously thrombosed segments without significant residual occlusive thrombus. This case is presented because of the uncommon combination of extensive bilateral lower limb and iliocaval thrombosis with acute PE and pulmonary infarction in the early postpartum period in a patient with heterozygous Factor V Leiden. It highlights how postpartum hypercoagulability may interact with inherited thrombophilia to produce extensive multisite thrombosis and emphasizes the importance of early recognition, severity-based risk stratification, and coordinated multidisciplinary management.

Venous Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral deep vein thrombosis (DVT) involving the iliac veins, right external iliac vein, infrarenal inferior vena cava (IVC), and right popliteal vein, with left popliteal involvement.

title: Preoperative Nutritional Testing Before Midfoot Fusion Is Infrequent, and With the Numbers Available, No Association Between Hypoalbuminemia and Postoperative Complications Could Be Detected: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate nutrition is essential for wound healing and postoperative recovery. Preoperative screening may identify high-risk patients and improve outcomes. This study aimed to determine whether abnormal preoperative nutritional laboratory values are associated with 90-day and 1-year complications including pseudarthrosis following midfoot fusion.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study using the TriNetX research network of more than 147 million patients, evaluating patients undergoing midfoot fusion with available preoperative nutritional laboratory values. Rates of preoperative laboratory testing were assessed, followed by propensity score-matched analyses comparing patients with abnormal and normal values. Ninety-day and 1-year postoperative complications were evaluated.

RESULTS: A total of 5667 patients underwent midfoot fusion. Preoperative nutritional laboratory markers were infrequently obtained (albumin 58.9%, leukocytes 36.0%, transferrin 3.2%, and prealbumin 1.9%) and often within normal limits (albumin 89.9%, leukocytes 99.5%, transferrin 79.7%, and prealbumin 91.0%). With the numbers available, no association could be detected between preoperative hypoalbuminemia and 90-day wound disruption (risk ratio [RR] 1.10, 95% CI 0.61-1.98), SSI (SSI; RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.54-1.68), hardware infection (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.70-2.56), return to emergency department (ED; RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.70-1.59), or readmission (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.88-1.45). With the numbers available, no association could be detected at 1 year postoperatively for pseudarthrosis (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.55-2.07), wound disruption (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.64-1.68), SSI (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.64-1.67), hardware infection (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.71-1.83), return to ED (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.83-1.39), readmission (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.95-1.46), hardware removal (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.66-1.71), pneumonia (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.36-1.71), and venous thromboembolism (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.60-2.52).

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative nutritional laboratory markers are infrequently obtained and are rarely abnormal when measured. With the numbers available, no association could be detected between preoperative hypoalbuminemia and increased 90-day or 1-year complications including pseudarthrosis following midfoot fusion.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

This study aimed to determine whether abnormal preoperative nutritional laboratory values are associated with 90-day and 1-year complications including pseudarthrosis following midfoot fusion.

title: Lymphatic Embolisation and Lymphangiography for Post-operative Inguinal Lymphorrhoea.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Inguinal lymphorrhoea is a well recognised complication of vascular surgery that is often refractory to conservative management. Moreover, repeated surgical intervention may increase the risk of wound contamination, recurrent lymphorrhoea, and delayed recovery. This Case Report evaluated the efficacy of lymphangiography and lymphatic embolisation as minimally invasive alternatives for managing refractory post-operative inguinal lymphorrhoea.

REPORT: The cases of four patients (aged 69 - 79 years) who developed refractory lymphorrhoea following arterial procedures, including common femoral artery cannulation and thromboendarterectomy, were reviewed. After conservative treatment or initial surgical management failed, lymphangiography was performed using ultrasound guided intranodal injection of iodised oil. In two patients, lymphatic embolisation was additionally performed using n-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate diluted with iodised oil in a ratio at 1:3 to 1:4. Fluoroscopic guidance enabled precise localisation of lymphatic leakage points. Lymphatic drainage was maintained using a pigtail catheter with continuous negative pressure. Lymphorrhoea resolved in all patients, and drainage catheters were removed within three - 13 days. No recurrence was observed during 10 - 30 months of follow up.

DISCUSSION: Lymphangiography and lymphatic embolisation may be effective, minimally invasive therapeutic options for refractory post-operative inguinal lymphorrhoea. These procedures facilitate the precise localisation and closure of lymphatic leaks, shorten recovery time, and help avoid surgical re-exploration of the groin and its associated risks.

Moreover, repeated surgical intervention may increase the risk of wound contamination, recurrent lymphorrhoea, and delayed recovery. title: Inflammatory bowel disease and the heart: how trained immunity shapes cardiovascular outcomes.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic relapsing intestinal inflammatory disorder. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death in patients with IBD, with elevated risks of myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, and venous thromboembolism that are independent of traditional risk factors. Disease activity and histological inflammation independently predict major adverse cardiovascular events, and Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis differ in cardiovascular risk profiles. This residual risk points to immune mechanisms that remain unclear. Trained immunity (TI), an innate immune memory induced by epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, may link chronic intestinal inflammation to cardiovascular injury. This review integrates epidemiological and mechanistic evidence, outlines cardiovascular risk features in IBD, examines the molecular basis of TI and its roles in atherosclerosis, myocardial injury, and heart failure, and evaluates candidate biomarkers and targeted therapeutic strategies. We also discuss current limitations and challenges in clinical translation and propose future research directions, to inform mechanistic studies and clinical interventions for IBD-associated CVD.

Disease activity and histological inflammation independently predict major adverse cardiovascular events, and Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis differ in cardiovascular risk profiles.

title: Noninvasive hemodynamics of nonthrombotic iliac vein lesions are disturbed in patients with a history of deep vein thrombosis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Nonthrombotic iliac vein lesions (NIVLs) are thought to be associated with deep vein thrombosis (DVT), yet most individuals with NIVL never develop thrombotic complications. This study assessed whether ultrasound-derived hemodynamic measurements differ between NIVL patients with and without a history of DVT, and whether these hemodynamic measurements better discriminate DVT history than percent stenosis alone.

METHODS: We performed a retrospective case control study of patients evaluated at a tertiary academic referral center between 2022 and 2025 who underwent pelvic venous duplex ultrasound imaging. Patients with left common iliac vein (LCIV) stenoses greater than 20% were included and categorized by history of left lower-extremity DVT. Exclusion criteria included concurrent DVT or previous venous stenting. Ultrasound images were digitized to obtain vessel diameters and spectral Doppler velocities in the iliac veins. Mean velocity, peak velocity, flow rate, shear rate, and ipsilateral and contralateral ratios were calculated. Continuous variables were compared using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, with statistical significance defined as P < .05.

RESULTS: Forty-five patients were included, comprising nine patients with previous DVT, and 36 without. Among all metrics, velocity-based metrics at the compressed LCIV showed the strongest associations with a history of previous DVT, including ipsilateral velocity ratio (log2 fold change [FC], -1.539; P = .007), peak velocity (log2FC, -0.999; P = .002), and mean velocity (log2FC, -0.989; P = .002). Differences in percent stenosis were statistically significant but less discriminative than velocity-based metrics (log2FC, 0.363; P = .033). Composite metrics such as flow rate and shear rate demonstrated weaker discrimination. Dimensionality reduction analysis revealed distinct clustering based on multivariate hemodynamic features between patients with and without a history of DVT.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with NIVL, decreased velocity through the LCIV at the compression point was the strongest predictor of previous DVT, whereas percent stenosis was less discriminative. This study suggests that ultrasound-derived hemodynamic assessment can potentially provide a functional framework for risk stratification in patients with NIVL, but further prospective studies are needed to validate its clinical utility.

This study assessed whether ultrasound-derived hemodynamic measurements differ between NIVL patients with and without a history of DVT, and whether these hemodynamic measurements better discriminate DVT history than percent stenosis alone. METHODS: We performed a retrospective case control study of patients evaluated at a tertiary academic referral center between 2022 and 2025 who underwent pelvic venous duplex ultrasound imaging.

title: A pilot study of the InVera Infusion Device: Twelve-month outcomes in the treatment of incompetent saphenous veins.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The InVera Infusion Device (IVID; InVera Medical) is a novel catheter designed for the delivery of sclerosant agents during nonthermal, nontumescent ablation of incompetent superficial truncal veins of the lower extremity. This device pilot study aimed to evaluate the technical success, safety, and 12-month clinical outcome.

METHODS: A single-center, prospective pilot study enrolled 10 patients with primary symptomatic axial reflux who underwent chemical ablation procedures with sclerosant delivery using the IVID. Primary outcomes assessed were technical procedural success, adverse events, revised Venous Clinical Severity Score (rVCSS), patient-reported outcomes based on a Heaviness, Achiness, Swelling, Throbbing, and Itching (HASTI) symptom questionnaire, and anatomical success rates from duplex ultrasound examination at baseline, 1 and 8 weeks, 3, 6, and 12 months postprocedure. Baseline and 12-month postprocedures were compared for both the rVCSS and the HASTI results using a paired t-test and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test respectively.

RESULTS: Technical procedural success was 100%. There were no device-related adverse events or serious adverse events including no deep vein thrombosis recorded throughout the follow-up period. Clinician assessed rVCSS and patient reported HASTI scores both showed statistically significant reductions from baseline to 12 months (adjusted P = .03 for both). Ultrasound-based anatomical assessment at 12 months demonstrated elimination of abnormal reflux and complete or partial occlusion in 90% of patients.

CONCLUSIONS: The IVID provides a safe and effective technique for the delivery of sclerosant agents as part of the management of incompetent saphenous veins, demonstrating favorable 12-month anatomical, clinical and patient-reported outcomes in this pilot cohort.

This device pilot study aimed to evaluate the technical success, safety, and 12-month clinical outcome. METHODS: A single-center, prospective pilot study enrolled 10 patients with primary symptomatic axial reflux who underwent chemical ablation procedures with sclerosant delivery using the IVID.

title: Systematic review of devices, designs, and trials for the treatment of deep venous reflux.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Chronic venous insufficiency is driven primarily by venous reflux and affects nearly one-third of adults. Although superficial reflux is effectively treated with ablation, therapeutic options for deep venous reflux (DVR) remain limited. Despite decades of innovation, no prosthetic or bioprosthetic venous valve has achieved U.S. regulatory approval. We systematically reviewed device strategies, clinical and hemodynamic outcomes, complications, and barriers to translation for devices designed to treat DVR.

METHODS: We conducted a PROSPERO-registered systematic review (CRD420251101761) of six databases from inception through February 2026, including in vivo animal and human studies evaluating prosthetic or bioprosthetic devices for DVR. Studies of native valve repair or autotransplantation were excluded. The primary outcome for human studies was clinical improvement, and secondary outcomes included patency, procedural complications, valvular function, and thrombosis.

RESULTS: Of 516 records identified, 15 met inclusion criteria: eight human and seven animal studies. Two principal strategies were identified: intraluminal valve restoration and external compression, with approximately 40% of devices delivered percutaneously or endovenously. In human studies, technical success ranged from 87.7% to 100%, patency from 67% to 100%, and perioperative complication rates from 0% to 44%, consisting primarily of bleeding, wound infection, and valve thrombosis. Valve occlusion occurred in up to 28% of animal implants and 18% to 22% of select human cohorts. One perioperative death occurred in animal studies; none were reported in human studies. Among human studies, valve competency assessment methods varied substantially. Reported competency ranged from 0% to 92%, reflecting heterogeneity in imaging modalities and definitions. Discordance between anatomic patency, duplex-derived reflux reduction, and clinical improvement was frequently observed. In contemporary multicenter trial data, fewer than half of patients met predefined reflux-reduction end points despite high device patency and substantial clinical improvement, highlighting discordance between anatomic, hemodynamic, and patient-centered outcomes. By 1 year, pain had improved in up to 97% of patients; revised Venous Clinical Severity Scores decreased by 37% to 81%, with clinically meaningful (≥3-point) improvement in up to 84.6%; and ulcer healing ranged from 67% to 100%. Longer follow-up extended to 2 years in animal studies and up to 11 years in human series with various outcomes reported.

CONCLUSIONS: Several devices developed for DVR have demonstrated technical feasibility and symptom improvement. However, the risk of thrombosis, the marginal impact on valvular function, and the lack of standardization and selection of adequate end points in the measurement of results remain major barriers to regulatory approval. Standardized composite end points integrating objective hemodynamic measures with patient-centered outcomes are essential to advance durable DVR device development and clinical translation.

title: Admission C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio is associated with early major amputation after minor amputation in patients with infected foot wounds.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Minor amputation is commonly performed as a limb-salvage procedure for infected foot wounds; however, some patients experience early limb-salvage failure and progress to major amputation. Reliable biomarkers predicting early failure remain limited.

PURPOSE: To evaluate whether the admission C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) is associated with major amputation within 90 days after minor amputation in patients with infected foot wounds.

STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

METHODS: Patients who underwent minor amputation for infected foot wounds between March 2005 and September 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Of 358 screened patients, 257 met the inclusion criteria. Admission CAR was calculated from C-reactive protein and serum albumin levels. The primary outcome was major amputation within 90 days. Univariable logistic regression and multivariable Cox proportional hazards analyses were performed. Predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

RESULTS: Among 257 patients, 60 (23.3%) progressed to major amputation within 90 days. Higher admission CAR values were significantly associated with major amputation. CAR remained an independent predictor in multivariable analysis (hazard ratio 1.17; 95% confidence interval 1.05-1.31; p value = .004). Adding CAR improved the predictive performance of the baseline model (area under the curve .883 vs .810).

CONCLUSIONS: Admission CAR is a simple and independent factor associated with early major amputation after minor amputation and may help facilitate early risk stratification.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Minor amputation is commonly performed as a limb-salvage procedure for infected foot wounds; however, some patients experience early limb-salvage failure and progress to major amputation. Reliable biomarkers predicting early failure remain limited. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether the admission C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) is associated with major amputation within 90 days after minor amputation in patients with infected foot wounds.

title: Ultraselective N-Butyl Cyanoacrylate Embolization of an Arteriobiliary Fistula After Transjugular Liver Biopsy With Preservation of Parent Arterial Flow.
abstract: Hemobilia is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of transjugular liver biopsy (TJLB). An arteriobiliary fistula associated with a hepatic arterial pseudoaneurysm may require prompt endovascular treatment. We report the case of a 17-year-old male who underwent TJLB to evaluate liver dysfunction in the presence of coagulopathy. Two days later, he developed abdominal pain and hyperbilirubinemia. Although his hemoglobin level was initially unchanged, progressive anemia subsequently developed despite blood transfusion. Computed tomography revealed a 3-mm pseudoaneurysm adjacent to the posterior sectoral branch of the right hepatic artery and findings suggestive of hemobilia. Five days after TJLB, ultraselective angiography confirmed communication between the pseudoaneurysm and the bile duct. Subsequent ultraselective embolization with a mixture of N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) and Lipiodol achieved complete occlusion of the fistula while preserving posterior sectoral arterial flow. Minimal migration of the NBCA-Lipiodol cast into a peripheral bile duct occurred during embolization. Abdominal pain resolved, and bilirubin levels returned to baseline within five days. The radiopaque component of the migrated cast was no longer visible on follow-up CT, and subsequent magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed no intrabiliary filling defects. No clinically significant biliary complications were observed during 28 months of follow-up. This case illustrates the feasibility of ultraselective NBCA embolization when coil isolation is limited by vascular anatomy, while emphasizing the risk of intrabiliary migration and the need for follow-up.
englishSummary: Hemobilia is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of transjugular liver biopsy (TJLB). An arteriobiliary fistula associated with a hepatic arterial pseudoaneurysm may require prompt endovascular treatment. We report the case of a 17-year-old male who underwent TJLB to evaluate liver dysfunction in the presence of coagulopathy.
